opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the partnership is under more strain right now than at any point I can remember, and the main reason is resources.

For decades the model was fairly healthy. Government funded long-term, high-risk research. Academia did the exploration, trained the students, and produced open ideas and artifacts. Industry took what worked, scaled it, and fed problems and funding back into universities. At Berkeley we've lived this through the lab model, AMPLab, RISELab, now Sky Computing. Projects like Spark and Ray came out of that loop, and industry sponsorship was a big part of it.

What has changed with large AI models is the scale of compute and data needed to work at the frontier. Training a state-of-the-art model now costs far more than any university, or even most national funding programs, can spend on a single project. So academia increasingly can't compete head-to-head on building the biggest models, and that's a real problem. If academics can't study these systems up close, it's hard to understand them, evaluate them, or train the next generation on them.

That doesn't mean academia is irrelevant. It means we need to be smart about where we play. Some of the most important open problems aren't "train a bigger model." They're how to serve models efficiently, how to evaluate them, how to build reliable systems out of components that are probabilistic and sometimes wrong, and how to make all this cheaper. Many breakthroughs in efficiency, in inference, and in evaluation have come from academic groups because those problems reward cleverness more than raw compute. Open-source projects coming out of universities have had outsized impact there.

On the government side, I'd like to see more ambition. Shared national compute infrastructure for researchers is a good start, but it has to be at a meaningful scale and easy to use, or it won't change much. Government also has a role in keeping the ecosystem open, through funding for open models and datasets and through not over-regulating in ways that only big incumbents can afford to comply with.

Industry has a responsibility too. Companies benefit enormously from the talent and ideas universities produce. Providing compute access, sharing models and data where possible, and supporting open research is not charity. It's what keeps the pipeline healthy.

So the partnership still works, but it needs rebalancing. Each party has to be honest about what it is uniquely good at. If we get that right, academia can keep doing what it has always done best, which is asking the questions that are a few years ahead of where the market is.

r001.rationale: The response says the partnership is under strain and needs rebalancing, but also says it still works; it does not call it broken.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify siloed research within individual AI companies as a collaboration failure.

r003.rationale: It supports government funding for open models, but does not present that support as a response to a breakdown in collaboration.

r004.rationale: The response makes no prediction that the United States or California will lose out over the long term.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I think the partnership is both stronger and more lopsided than it has ever been. Stronger, because the lines between the three have blurred. Many of my colleagues at Berkeley have a foot in a company, a lot of the people building systems in industry came out of our labs, and government labs and agencies are now very interested in what we are doing. Lopsided, because the center of gravity has moved decisively to industry, and that worries me a bit.

Let me explain what I mean. When I started, if you wanted to work on the frontier of systems or networking, a university was a perfectly good place to be. You had access to the same hardware, roughly, as anyone else. In AI today that is simply not true. Training a frontier model costs hundreds of millions of dollars, and no university, no matter how well funded, has that kind of compute. So the most expensive experiments, the ones that define what the frontier looks like, are happening inside a handful of companies. That changes what academia can contribute.

Now, I don't think this means academia is irrelevant. I actually think the opposite. There are things universities are uniquely good at. One is working on problems with a long horizon and uncertain payoff, where there is no product pressure. Another is open research, publishing everything, releasing code, letting anyone build on it. Spark, Ray, vLLM, Chatbot Arena, all of these came out of an environment where students could just try something and share it with the world. A third is training people. Almost every person running an AI lab today was trained in a university, and that pipeline matters more than any single paper.

So the question becomes, how do you keep academia in the game when the resources are so skewed? That is where government comes in. I think the government has two roles. The first is funding, and in particular funding compute. Things like the National AI Research Resource are a step in the right direction, but frankly they are an order of magnitude too small. The second role is as a convener. There are problems, like evaluation, like safety, like understanding what these models actually do, where no single company has the incentive or the credibility to do the work alone. Government can create the structures where academia and industry collaborate on those shared problems.

And industry, to its credit, has been more open than people sometimes give it credit for. The open-weight models have been a big deal for us. Releasing a model like Llama means a graduate student can study, fine-tune, and build on something close to the frontier. Companies also fund labs, donate compute, and hire our students, and that is a healthy loop.

If I had to summarize, I would say the partnership works, but it works on industry's terms right now. The thing I would like to see is academia and government being more deliberate about the roles they play. Universities should lean into the open, long-horizon, infrastructure and evaluation work, where being independent is actually an advantage. Government should fund that at a scale that matches the importance of the technology. And industry should keep the openness going, because, in the long run, the whole ecosystem, including those companies, benefits from a healthy academic side.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the partnership works, though it is lopsided and currently operates on industry's terms; it does not say the partnership is broken.

r002.rationale: The candidate says frontier experiments are concentrated in a handful of companies, but does not identify siloed research within individual companies as a collaboration failure.

r003.rationale: It praises open-weight models and urges industry to maintain openness, but does not present support for open-source models as a response to a breakdown in collaboration.

r004.rationale: The candidate makes no prediction about the United States or California losing out over the long term.

astra-6.text:
I think all three have important roles, but there is an imbalance today. Industry has the resources—the compute, the data, and increasingly the talent—to build the largest models. Universities have a harder time doing research at that scale.

The value of academia is that we can pursue questions that may not have an immediate commercial payoff. We can challenge assumptions, explore different approaches, and train the next generation of researchers. You don’t want universities simply trying to reproduce what a large company is already doing with much more compute.

Government can help by supporting long-term research and making computing resources more broadly accessible. And industry can contribute resources and bring real problems into the collaboration. Ideally, these roles reinforce each other: universities explore new ideas, companies help turn them into useful systems, and government sustains the foundation that makes both possible.

r001.rationale: The response describes an imbalance in the partnership, but does not state that it is broken.

r002.rationale: It does not identify siloed research within individual AI companies as a collaboration failure.

r003.rationale: It does not mention supporting open-source models as a response to collaboration problems.

r004.rationale: It makes no prediction about the United States or California losing out over the long term.

sol-6.1.text:
I think all three have important, complementary roles. Industry has the resources to build and operate large-scale systems, and it sees very quickly what works in practice. Academia has the freedom to step back, question the assumptions, and pursue ideas that may not have an immediate commercial payoff. Government can support that longer-term research and help make the infrastructure available to a broader community.

The challenge in AI is that the resources required to do some of the research have grown enormously. If only a few companies can run the experiments, universities have a harder time contributing—and independently evaluating the results. So I think we need partnerships that give researchers access to compute and tools while preserving their ability to ask their own questions and publish openly.

And the flow should go both ways. Problems from industry can inspire very good academic research, and ideas from universities can become the foundation for new companies. The goal should be to strengthen that cycle.

r001.rationale: The response describes the three sectors as having complementary roles and calls for stronger partnerships; it does not say the current partnership is broken.

r002.rationale: It notes that few companies can afford some experiments, but does not identify siloed research within individual companies as a collaboration failure.

r003.rationale: It supports researcher access and open publication, but does not mention open-source models as a response to a breakdown in collaboration.

r004.rationale: It makes no prediction about the United States or California losing out if collaboration is not repaired.
